name: Austrian Dominoes
description: Austrian Dominoes is a unique European variant traditionally played with a Double-Eight set. Its most striking features are the complete removal of all double tiles and a 'brick-layer' tableau formation where tiles are matched side-by-side rather than end-to-end. It is a strategic draw game where players value 'heavier' tiles early in the round.

history.origins: Documented in Vienna as early as 1830, Austrian Dominoes reflects the Central European preference for Double-Eight sets over the more common Double-Six set used in the West.
timeline: 1830: F. Tendler publishes 'Verstand und GlÃ¼ck im Bunde', describing the game with 45 tiles.
1960: Fritz Beck standardizes the 36-tile 'No-Double' variant in 'Domino in vielen Spielarten'.
Present: Remains a traditional past-time in Austrian card clubs and cafes.
history.cultural: Often played in a 'Buki' format (4 players) in rural Austria.
history.evolution: The removal of doubles removes the 'spinners' and the high-point anchors typical of Caribbean or American games, shifting focus to pure numerical matching.

setup.deck: 36 tiles. To prepare, take a Double-Eight set (45 tiles) and discard all 9 doubles (0-0, 1-1... up to 8-8).
setup.dealing: 2 players: 8-9 tiles each. 3 players: 7 tiles each. 4 players: 8 tiles each. Remaining tiles form the 'Stamm' (Boneyard).

rules.objective: To be the first player to reach 100 points across multiple rounds.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Leading**: The player with the heaviest tile (8-7 being the heaviest in this set) leads first. 2. **Matching**: On your turn, you must place a tile where one of its ends matches an available end on the board. 3. **The Draw**: If you cannot play, you must draw from the boneyard until you find a playable tile. (Common house rule: maximum of 3 draws). 4. **Passing**: If the boneyard is empty and you cannot play, you pass. 5. **Ending**: A round ends when one player 'Dominoes' (empties their hand) or when the game is blocked.
keyRules: No Doubles: The absence of doubles means every tile is distinct and has two different numbers.
The 8-7 Lead: The highest tile in play (8-7) always starts the first hand.
Brick Formation: The tableau grows in two directions from the starting tile, but specifically in a side-by-side matching manner.

strategy.basic: Keep a variety of numbers in your hand. Since there are no doubles, you don't have to worry about 'blocking' your own suits in the same way.
strategy.intermediate: High-Pip Management: Early in the game, try to play your 8s and 7s. If someone else dominoes, you don't want to be caught with high-counting tiles in your hand.
strategy.advanced: Boneyard Counting: Since there are only 36 tiles and you know exactly which ones are missing (the doubles), you can more accurately track which tiles are left in the boneyard vs in opponents' hands.
tips: If you are playing the 4-player block variant, remember that there is no boneyard. Information is perfect if you can track all 36 tiles.
The 'Brick' layout can sometimes be confusing; visualize the ends as 'slots' that must match.

variations.name: Buki
variations.description: A 4-player block version where all titles are dealt out and no drawing is allowed.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Buki is a related gambling-style variant; stake handling and detailed payments are not yet modeled as engine overrides in this file.

scoring.winCondition: First player to 100 points wins the game.

synthesis.shortDescription: Discover the traditional domino game of Central Europe. With the nine doubles removed, strategies shift and the unique side-matching bricks create a beautiful, tactical tableau. Master the 36-tile set and lead with your heaviest pips.
